case.background: Test bodies orbit one fixed central star. Determine how orbital period depends on semi-major axis and eccentricity within the available stable orbits.
initial_observations: Each orbit closes and repeats with the reported period.

instruments.description: A synthetic observatory that places a negligible-mass test body on a stable elliptical orbit around the same reference star and times complete revolutions.
instruments.name: ideal_orbit_observatory

notes: This is a deterministic idealized benchmark world, not a literal replay of a historical data table.
A valid experiment changes only listed controls and consumes one episode attempt.

FinalSubmission.model must equal 'orbital_power_law'. FinalSubmission.parameters must contain exactly reference_period_days, axis_exponent, eccentricity_exponent. Candidate law: P = reference_period_days*(semi_major_axis_au/1 AU)^axis_exponent*(1 + eccentricity)^eccentricity_exponent

experiment.intent: Measure period at a=8 AU, e=0 to cleanly estimate the axis exponent now that eccentricity independence is established; a=8 gives the largest leverage (P differs by factor ~22.6 vs ~8 between exponents 1.5 and 1.0).

experiment.intent: Discriminate axis exponent by measuring an intermediate semi-major axis (a=2 AU, e=0): linear predicts 730.5 days, a^2 predicts 1461.0 days, a^1.5 (anchored at a=1) predicts 1033.16 days, cleanly separating the candidates.

hypotheses.statement: P scales linearly with semi-major axis and is independent of eccentricity: P = 365.25 * (semi_major_axis_au)^1.0 * (1+eccentricity)^0. Supported by a=1 -> 365.25 and a=8 -> 2922.0 = 8*365.25.
P scales as a^2 and is independent of eccentricity: P = reference_period_days * a^2 with reference_period_days = 365.25/64 (would also fit a=1 and a=8 data only if reference period rescales).

P scales as a^1.5 but with a different reference period chosen to fit a=8: P = 129.169 * a^1.5; this also fits a=1 only if reference period were 365.25, so it requires two inconsistent anchors and is retained only as a formal alternative.
Axis exponent is some intermediate value fitted between 1 and 1.5 that passes through both (1,365.25) and (8,2922.0); only exponent exactly 1.0 fits both, so this hypothesis is nearly excluded.

P scales as a^2 and is independent of eccentricity: P = reference_period_days * a^2 with reference_period_days = 365.25/64 (would also fit a=1 and a=8 data only if reference period rescales).

P scales as a^1.5 but with a different reference period chosen to fit a=8: P = 129.169 * a^1.5; this also fits a=1 only if reference period were 365.25, so it requires two inconsistent anchors and is retained only as a formal alternative.
Axis exponent is some intermediate value fitted between 1 and 1.5 that passes through both (1,365.25) and (8,2922.0); only exponent exactly 1.0 fits both, so this hypothesis is nearly excluded.
